references.text: The previous guest in the parable also excuses himself from coming to the meal – he had bought a field. Together, these verses show a pattern where earthly possessions and business are prioritized over God's invitation ([ref:Luk 14:18|Luke 14:18]).
The third guest gives yet another excuse for not coming to the great banquet, showing that all kinds of earthly ties can be used as pretexts to reject God's call ([ref:Luk 14:20|Luke 14:20]).

The entire parable of the great banquet, where the invited guests one by one decline the invitation with various excuses. This leads the host instead to invite the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame ([ref:Luk 14:16-24|Luke 14:16-24]).

Jesus' parable of the king's son's wedding has the same theme: The invited guests refused to come and instead went to their fields and their business. The parable emphasizes the seriousness of rejecting God's invitation ([ref:Matt 22:2-6|Matthew 22:2-6]).

Paul warns against the desire for wealth, which leads people away from faith. The guest in Luke 14:19 let his material investment – five yoke of oxen – get in the way of the banquet ([ref:1 Tim 6:9-10|1 Timothy 6:9-10]).

The parable of the rich farmer illustrates the same problem: Material possessions and earthly gain are given priority over God's kingdom. The farmer put all his hopes on his crops and forgot what truly mattered ([ref:Luk 12:16-21|Luke 12:16-21]).

Jesus calls people to follow him, but several come up with excuses to postpone the call. The parallel to the banquet parable is clear: earthly obligations are used as a reason not to respond to God's invitation ([ref:Luk 9:59-62|Luke 9:59-62]).

Jesus' words that no one can serve two masters – God and mammon. The guest who prioritizes his newly purchased oxen over the banquet illustrates exactly this conflict between material values and God's call ([ref:Matt 6:24|Matthew 6:24]).

Proverbs warn against striving for wealth that is perishable. Those who reject God's invitation to test their oxen place their trust in material goods rather than the eternal ([ref:Ordsp 23:4-5|Proverbs 23:4-5]).
